On successful completion of this course, students will be able to:

Knowledge

  • Apply foundational concepts from the humanities to propose potential solutions or frameworks for modern global challenges.
  • Critically analyse how philosophical and humanistic ideas inform contemporary debates regarding social justice, technological ethics, and global sustainability.
  • Analyse how humanities perspectives contribute to understanding contemporary global challenges reflected in the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals.
  • Synthesise diverse disciplinary perspectives within the humanities to address a complex societal problem.
Skills
  • Interpret and evaluate scholarly literature, documentaries, and other cultural sources using conceptual and analytical frameworks from the humanities.
  • Construct well-reasoned arguments that integrate theoretical perspectives with empirical examples and contemporary case studies.
Character
  • Demonstrate intellectual curiosity and openness towards diverse perspectives, cultures, and worldviews.
  • Reflect critically on one's own assumptions, values, and responsibilities as a member of an interconnected global society.
  • Engage respectfully and thoughtfully with complex, controversial, and ethically challenging questions affecting humanity.

Contemporary societies face unprecedented challenges, including climate change, artificial intelligence and ethics, health inequalities, polarisation, technological transformation, and opportunities, such as global migration, growing linguistic, social, and cultural diversity. Addressing these issues requires more than technological or economic interventions. We need to critically reflect on the underlying ideas, values, and assumptions that shape human societies. The humanities provide conceptual frameworks for examining fundamental questions about human existence, self-understanding, knowledge construction, and coexistence in complex, interconnected societies.

This interdisciplinary course introduces students to influential ideas in the humanities by linking classical philosophical questions to contemporary societal challenges. Drawing on perspectives from cultural studies, intercultural communication, philosophy, sociology, and sociolinguistics, the course examines concepts such as identity, belonging, language, phenomenology, justice, democracy, health, technology, sustainability, and human responsibility. Through critical reading, discussion, case studies, documentaries, and reflective assignments, students develop the intellectual tools to analyse complex global issues from multiple perspectives and to recognise the significance of the humanities in understanding contemporary society.
